message.content:
The last common ancestor of a lion (Panthera leo) and a zebra (Equus quagga) is a **placental mammal that lived roughly 70–90 million years ago**.  
It would have been a small, probably insect‑eating animal that belonged to the clade **Laurasiatheria**, the group that later gave rise to both the carnivores (Carnivora) and the odd‑tailed ungulates (Perissodactyla). In other words, the lion and zebra share a very ancient mammalian ancestor that predates the split between the major lineages that eventually became cats and horses.

Actually both are placental mammals. The last common ancestor of all placental mammals is the eutherian ancestor. Wait, the phylogeny: Placentalia splits into Afrotheria, Xenarthra, and Boreoeutheria. Boreoeutheria splits into Euarchontoglires and Laurasiatheria. Laurasiatheria splits into several orders: Chiroptera, Cetartiodactyla, Eulipotyphla, Perissodactyla, and Carnivora. So the last common ancestor of Carnivora and Perissodactyla would be the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria, which is a mammal that lived about 90-100 million years ago. So the answer: the last common ancestor of lion and zebra is a small, probably insectivorous mammal that lived in the late Cretaceous or early Paleogene, part of the Laurasiatheria clade.
